title: Reading evidence: packets, Linux, Windows and network sensors
summary: Read four kinds of evidence from one night at a clinic: a Linux server's auth log and processes, a packet capture, Zeek connection logs and Windows event logs. Find a brute force, a script download, a beacon and a hop to a reception PC, then write a host triage note and a network finding.
titlePrefix: Reading evidence: packets, Linux, Windows and network sensors
rubric: Evidence hashed and listed before any analysis
Brute force and the successful login found in auth.log, with the commands used
What happened after the login: the download, the cron job and the running process
Packets: the download and the beacon found with display filters, the filters written down
Zeek conn.log: who talked to whom, including the connection to the reception PC
Windows: failed and successful logons and the share access, with event IDs
IDS rules that catch the download and the beacon, and nothing normal
Host triage note and network finding: facts kept apart from guesses, next steps with owners
handin: A host triage note for appt01 and a one-page network finding, each with the commands and filters you used.

script.intro: Hello, and welcome to Reading evidence. Every analyst job, whatever its title, comes down to reading four kinds of evidence: a server's logs, the packets on the wire, a network sensor's summary, and a Windows event log. Each one tells part of the story, and none of them tells all of it. In this seminar we follow one night at Tamarind Health, a chain of clinics in Pune, through all four. Someone guesses a password on the appointments server, gets in, downloads a program, and reaches across the network to a reception PC full of patient scans. You'll find every step of that yourself, with grep, a packet viewer, a Zeek log and the Windows Security log, and by the end you'll write it up so the next person can act. It's a long night, so let's be methodical.

steps.say: Step one: take stock of the evidence. Every case starts the same way. Read the README so you know the machines, the addresses and the time zone. Then list what you were given, and hash it before you open anything. A hash is a fingerprint of a file. If anyone ever asks whether the evidence changed in your hands, the hashes are your proof. The Linux cell lists every file and prints a SHA-256 hash for each one.
steps.after: The README sets the scene. It's the night of the fifth to the sixth of November 2026, and every time is UTC. appt01, at 10.30.1.20, is the MediBook appointments server, running Ubuntu. Its SSH port is forwarded from the internet so the software vendor can support it, which is exactly the kind of decision that comes back to bite. rcp-pc03, at 10.30.2.33, is a reception PC with a share called Scans, full of patient scans and referrals. We have eight files: the server's auth.log, its process list and crontab, a script recovered from its tmp folder, a packet capture from the core switch, a Zeek connection log, the reception PC's Security log, and the README. And an IDS alert started all this at 01:20:11: a possible script download by Wget. Copy the hash list into your notes. Answer the questions: eight files, and appt01 is 10.30.1.20.

steps.say: Step two: Linux, who was knocking. Port 22 is open to the internet, so auth.log is full of strangers trying passwords. Three small commands do all the work. grep minus c counts the failed passwords. Then grep minus o keeps just the from-address part of each line, sort puts identical addresses together, uniq minus c counts each one, and sort minus r n ranks them, biggest first. The last line does the same for the user names that were tried.
steps.after: Fifty failed passwords in total, and forty-six of them came from one address: 198.51.100.23. One address, dozens of guesses in a short time, that's a brute force. Now look at the names it tried. root, and names that don't exist on this server, like admin, test, ubnt, postgres and oracle, which auth.log marks as invalid user. Those come from a standard list attackers use. But one name does exist: vendor, tried sixteen times. That's the account the software company uses for support. An account that faces the internet and is protected only by a password is the weak point here. Answer the three questions: fifty failures, 198.51.100.23, and forty-six from that address.

steps.say: Step three: Linux, the login and what came next. A brute force only matters if it worked, so now we look for the word Accepted. Then we read everything that account did afterwards. sudo lines show each command run as root, because sudo logs the full command. Then we check the two places attackers hide so they can come back: a scheduled job, which Linux calls cron, and a running process. The cell prints the accepted logins, the sudo commands, the recovered script, the crontab and the matching processes.
steps.after: There are two Accepted lines. The first is deploy, logging in with a key from 10.30.0.15, the IT admin PC, at 00:40, as it does every night. That's normal, and it's worth saying so in your notes, so nobody wastes time on it. The second is vendor, from 198.51.100.23, with a password, at 01:19:44. That's our attacker. Twenty-six seconds later, at 01:20:10, sudo runs wget to fetch m.sh from cdn.patch-relay.example into a hidden file in tmp, and at 01:20:31 runs it as root. Read the recovered script. It uses curl to download a.bin, saves it as /usr/local/bin/.sysmon-agent, with a dot at the front so a normal listing hides it and a name chosen to look like monitoring software, and adds a cron line that runs it every ten minutes. The crontab confirms it: the nightly backup line is old and normal, the sysmon-agent line is new. And ps shows .sysmon-agent running as root since 01:21. That's persistence. One more sudo line, at 01:33: smbclient, connecting to a share called Scans on 10.30.2.33 as the user frontdesk. Hold on to that, we'll come back to it. Answer the questions: vendor, the path /usr/local/bin/.sysmon-agent, and 01:19:44.

steps.say: Step four: packets, the download. Logs tell you what a computer says happened. Packets show what actually crossed the wire. The capture is the core switch's mirror port from 01:15. In the packet viewer, a display filter keeps only the packets you ask for. We'll start with every HTTP request, then everything to or from the download server, and then the same question on the command line with tshark.
steps.after: http.request finds two requests, both to cdn.patch-relay.example at 203.0.113.77. The first fetches /m.sh with the User-Agent Wget, which matches the sudo line exactly. The second fetches /a.bin with the User-Agent curl/7.81.0, which matches the line inside the script. So the packets confirm the logs, and that matters: two independent sources telling the same story is much stronger than one. The second filter, ip.addr equals 203.0.113.77, shows every packet to and from that server, and if you follow the first stream you can read the script itself as it travelled. tshark prints the same two requests, one per line, which is how you'd do it on a server with no screen. Answer the questions: the host name is cdn.patch-relay.example, and a.bin was fetched by curl/7.81.0.

steps.say: Step five: packets, the beacon. After the download, appt01 keeps calling the same server, but now over TLS, which is encrypted. We can't read what it says. But two things are never encrypted: the timing of the connections, and the server name in the TLS Client Hello, called the SNI. A program that calls the same server at a fixed interval is a beacon: it's checking in for instructions. The first filter shows TLS to 203.0.113.77, and the second shows the DNS lookups for the patch-relay name.
steps.after: Look at the Time column. TLS Client Hellos to 203.0.113.77 at 01:21, 01:31 and 01:41. Exactly ten minutes apart. And what runs every ten minutes? The cron line the script added. So we can link the encrypted traffic to the program on disk without reading a single byte of it. Compare that with the other TLS on the network, to the patient portal and the backup server: those are internal, they go to known names, and they don't tick like a clock. Regular, external, and to a name nobody recognises: that's the shape of a beacon. Answer the question: ten minutes apart.

steps.say: Step six: network sensor, who talked to whom. Zeek is a network sensor that writes one line per connection: who opened it, to which address and port, which service, how long it lasted and how many bytes went each way. It's the fastest way to see a whole night at once. The fields are separated by tabs, so the cell uses awk with a tab as the separator to pull out who, to whom, which port and which service, and then counts each pair. The second command shows only the connections to 10.30.2.33.
steps.after: Read the counted pairs. appt01 opened five connections to 203.0.113.77: the two downloads on port 80 and the three beacons on 443, matching the packets exactly. Then the line that should make you sit up: appt01 to 10.30.2.33 on port 445, which is Windows file sharing. Why would an appointments server open a Windows share on a reception PC? It has no reason to. That's lateral movement: the attacker using the first machine to reach the next one. And the biggest transfer of the night? That's the nightly backup at 01:30, internal, to the backup server, as it is every night. Big doesn't mean bad, and saying so in your notes saves the next person a fright. Answer the questions: five connections, and 10.30.2.33.

steps.say: Step seven: Windows, the hop to reception. The reception PC saw those port 445 connections as logons, and Windows writes every logon to its Security log. Four event IDs tell the story. 4625 is a failed logon. 4624 is a successful one. Logon Type 3 means over the network, not at the keyboard. 5140 is a share being opened, and 5145 is a file in it being read. The event viewer filters the log by event ID and by the attacker's address, 10.30.1.20.
steps.after: From 01:33:10 to 01:33:50, nine failed logons from 10.30.1.20 for the account frontdesk, one every five seconds. That's another password guess, now against Windows. At 01:34:02, a successful logon, Logon Type 3, over the network. At 01:34:03 the Scans share is opened, and over the next minute six files are read: scan-0411, scan-0412, scan-0413, referral-0414, scan-0415 and lab-0416. Patient scans, a referral and a lab report. Notice the one 4625 at 03:31 on the fifth of November: that's Logon Type 2, the receptionist mistyping at the keyboard, and it isn't part of this. This is where the stakes change. Until now it was a compromised server. Now it's patient health data read by an attacker, and that brings the clinic's legal duties into play. Answer the questions: nine failed logons, the Scans share, and six files.

steps.say: Step eight: a sensor rule for next time. Finding an attack once is good. Making sure the next one raises an alert by itself is better. We'll turn what we found into two IDS rules that run on every packet. Rule one alerts when a server fetches something with Wget or curl. Rule two alerts on TLS to the beacon's server name. Then we run them on the capture and check two things: they catch the bad traffic, and they stay quiet on the portal, the backup and the database.
steps.after: Five alerts: rule one catches both downloads, and rule two catches all three beacons, and nothing fires on the internal traffic. That's a good rule: it catches what it should and nothing else. Now write one line on what each would miss. Rule one misses a download made with a renamed program or a browser-like User-Agent, but a real server rarely needs Wget or curl to reach the internet, so it's still worth having on servers. Rule two only knows one server name, and attackers change names easily. The more lasting sign is the timing, a call every ten minutes, which you can catch with the Zeek log instead. Answer the question: the two rules give five alerts.

steps.say: Step nine: write the triage note and the network finding. Two short documents carry all this to the next person: a host triage note for appt01, and a network finding for the hour from 01:00 to 02:00. Each one says what you checked, with the exact commands and filters, so anyone can repeat it, and each keeps facts apart from guesses.
steps.after: Read the model triage note. What fired: the IDS alert at 01:20:11. What I checked: the exact greps on auth.log, the crontab, the process list and the recovered script. What I found: the brute force, the vendor login at 01:19:44, the download, the persistence, and the hop to rcp-pc03. And the part that matters most, what I don't know yet. We have not analysed a.bin. Write exactly that, we have not analysed the binary, not it is probably ransomware. A guess in a triage note becomes a fact by the third person who reads it. Then the network finding: the five connections to 203.0.113.77, the ten-minute beacon, the 445 connection to reception, and the backup, explained as normal. Every next step has an owner, and every time is in UTC.

steps.say: Step ten: hand in. Hand in this notebook. It carries every answer, every tool result and both reports. Your teacher marks it with the rubric, and the certificate follows once it's scored.
steps.after: Before you press Hand in, check three things. Every time is UTC. Every fact says where you saw it. And the gaps, the binary we haven't analysed, whether anything left the network, are written down plainly.

script.outro: That's the night, from start to finish. A password guessed on an internet-facing account. A script downloaded and run as root. A program that hides, persists through cron and beacons every ten minutes. And a hop to a reception PC where six patient files were read. You found each step in a different kind of evidence, and the strongest findings were the ones where two sources agreed: sudo and the packets, cron and the beacon, Zeek and the Windows log. That's the skill: read each source carefully, then line them up on one clock. Next, in Log search and detection as code, you'll do the same at scale with a SIEM. Thank you for watching.

template.s:
# Reading evidence: packets, Linux, Windows and network sensors

Read four kinds of evidence from one night at a clinic: a Linux server's auth log and processes, a packet capture, Zeek connection logs and Windows event logs. Find a brute force, a script download, a beacon and a hop to a reception PC, then write a host triage note and a network finding.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `auth.log`, `capture.pcap`, `crontab.txt`, `eventlogs/Security.jsonl`, `ps.txt`, `README.txt`, `recovered/m.sh`, `zeek/conn.log`.

## 1. Take stock of the evidence

Start every case the same way: read the README, list what you were given, and hash it before you open anything. The hashes prove later that nobody changed the evidence after you received it.

- [ ] Read README.txt: which machines, which addresses, which times
- [ ] List every file
- [ ] Hash every file and keep the list

> Hint: `ls -R` lists folders inside folders. `sha256sum` prints one hash per file.

?> How many evidence files are there, including the README? :: sha256:2c624232cdd221771294dfbb310aca000a0df6ac8b66b696d90ef06fdefb64a3
?> What is the IP address of appt01? :: sha256:4b0ea0f668396f131ec196b64f8ec381999a084e3a47b8da2e5f755a65e184c4

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with ls.
template.a:
cd ~/case
ls -R
echo ---
sha256sum auth.log ps.txt crontab.txt capture.pcap README.txt recovered/m.sh zeek/conn.log eventlogs/Security.jsonl

template.s:
## 2. Linux: who was knocking

appt01 is open to the internet on port 22. `auth.log` records every SSH login, good or bad. Count the failures, then count them **by source address**: one address making dozens of guesses is a brute force.

- [ ] How many failed passwords in total?
- [ ] Which address made most of them, and how many?
- [ ] Which user names did it try? Which one is a real account here?

> Hint: `grep -o 'from [0-9.]*'` keeps only the address part of each line; `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` counts and ranks them.

?> How many failed passwords are in auth.log in total? :: sha256:1a6562590ef19d1045d06c4055742d38288e9e6dcd71ccde5cee80f1d5a774eb
?> Which address made the most failed attempts? :: sha256:bfeb4c6192985efa05e7fa0740ac45708a515e569e7edaec7fc060ff72b44a0c
?> How many failed attempts came from that address? :: sha256:25fc0e7096fc653718202dc30b0c580b8ab87eac11a700cba03a7c021bc35b0c

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with grep.
template.a:
cd ~/case
grep -c 'Failed password' auth.log
echo ---
grep 'Failed password' auth.log | grep -o 'from [0-9.]*' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
echo ---
grep 'Failed password' auth.log | grep -o 'for [a-z ]*from' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

template.s:
## 3. Linux: the login and what came next

A brute force only matters if it worked. Find the **Accepted** line, then read everything the account did afterwards: `sudo` lines show each command run as root. Then check the two things an attacker leaves to come back: a scheduled job and a running process.

- [ ] Which account logged in from 198.51.100.23, when, and with what (password or key)?
- [ ] Which commands did it run with sudo?
- [ ] What did the script change? Read recovered/m.sh
- [ ] Which cron line and which process are new?

> Hint: The deploy account logs in with a key from the IT admin PC every night; that one is normal. Compare the cron lines with what the script added.

?> Which account logged in with a password from 198.51.100.23? :: sha256:630ba09448af522154f38ef7685ef1f44b0f3e9430f80829a03ce24f400f3754
?> What file does the new cron job run? (full path) :: sha256:b57fa7460b593d55238865605d1856f2f10920d596db667477e2b06fc4ca7e6a
?> At what time (UTC, HH:MM:SS) did that login succeed? :: sha256:dcd0265553c98b2647b88d9fc0ae73807c06ce0d9ca87c75e1934436a0dd87f9

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with grep.
template.a:
cd ~/case
grep 'Accepted' auth.log
echo ---
grep 'sudo' auth.log | grep COMMAND
echo ---
cat recovered/m.sh
echo ---
cat crontab.txt
echo ---
grep -E 'sysmon|\.m\.sh' ps.txt

template.s:
## 4. Packets: the download

Now the wire. The capture is the core switch mirror from 01:15. In the packet viewer a **display filter** keeps only the packets you ask for. Start with every HTTP request, then everything to or from the download server, and follow the stream of the first download.

```tool packets
{"file": "capture.pcap", "f": "", "n": 2, "blank": ["f"], "a": {"f": "http.request"}}
```

```tool packets
{"file": "capture.pcap", "f": "", "n": 10, "blank": ["f"], "a": {"f": "ip.addr==203.0.113.77"}}
```

The Linux cell below asks tshark the same question on the command line.

- [ ] Which two files were fetched, from which host name?
- [ ] Which program fetched each one? (the User-Agent)
- [ ] What kind of file came back each time?

> Hint: The first request's User-Agent is Wget, which matches the sudo line. The second is curl, which matches the script.

?> Which host name served /m.sh? :: sha256:817ce8dbe01257e2e21aca4761c28838ae142340ef0c0e5ea0c955264c1246e4
?> Which User-Agent fetched /a.bin? :: sha256:288d55347fe66e2a73b6a951f78d3729876d7bc80cf71082a5ef4addbf753f8b

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with tshark.
template.a:
cd ~/case
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'http.request' -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent

template.s:
## 5. Packets: the beacon

After the download, appt01 keeps calling the same server over TLS. The content is encrypted, but the **timing** and the **server name** (SNI) are not. Regular calls at a fixed interval are a beacon: a program checking in for instructions.

```tool packets
{"file": "capture.pcap", "f": "", "n": 3, "blank": ["f"], "a": {"f": "tls and ip.dst==203.0.113.77"}}
```

```tool packets
{"file": "capture.pcap", "f": "", "n": 8, "blank": ["f"], "a": {"f": "dns.qry.name contains patch-relay"}}
```

- [ ] When does each TLS Client Hello to 203.0.113.77 start?
- [ ] How far apart are they? Does that match the cron line?
- [ ] Compare with the TLS to portal and backup: why are those normal?

> Hint: Look at the Time column. The cron line runs every ten minutes.

?> How many minutes apart are the TLS connections to 203.0.113.77? :: sha256:4a44dc15364204a80fe80e9039455cc1608281820fe2b24f1e5233ade6af1dd5

## 6. Network sensor: who talked to whom

Zeek writes one line per connection: who opened it, to which address and port, how long it lasted and how many bytes went each way. It's the fastest way to see the whole night at once. The fields are separated by tabs; the `#fields` line names them.

- [ ] List every pair: from, to, port, service, with a count
- [ ] How many connections did appt01 open to 203.0.113.77?
- [ ] Which internal machine did appt01 connect to on port 445 (Windows file sharing)? Why is that strange for an appointments server?
- [ ] Which connection moved the most bytes? Is it suspicious?

> Hint: Field 3 is id.orig_h (who opened it), 5 is id.resp_h, 6 is id.resp_p, 8 is service and 11 is resp_bytes. The biggest transfer is the nightly backup, which is internal and runs at 01:30 every night.

?> How many connections did appt01 open to 203.0.113.77? :: sha256:ef2d127de37b942baad06145e54b0c619a1f22327b2ebbcfbec78f5564afe39d
?> Which internal address did appt01 connect to on port 445? :: sha256:13dd5dc4e7aea0de7349cfd02701ce0836f6b9fbb32b4636f5086eda771a983a

# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
# Hint: the recording started with grep.
template.a:
cd ~/case/zeek
grep -v '^#' conn.log | awk -F'\t' '{print $3, "->", $5":"$6, $8}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
echo ---
grep -v '^#' conn.log | awk -F'\t' '$5=="10.30.2.33" {print $1, $3, $6, $12, $11}'

template.s:
## 7. Windows: the hop to reception

The reception PC saw those port 445 connections as **logons**. In the Security log, 4625 is a failed logon and 4624 a successful one; Logon Type 3 means over the network. 5140 is a share being opened and 5145 a file in it being read.

```tool events
{"file": "eventlogs/Security.jsonl", "ids": "", "q": "", "n": 9, "blank": ["ids", "src", "q"], "a": {"ids": "4625", "q": "10.30.1.20"}}
```

```tool events
{"file": "eventlogs/Security.jsonl", "ids": "", "q": "", "n": 8, "blank": ["ids", "src", "q"], "a": {"ids": "4624, 5140, 5145", "q": "10.30.1.20"}}
```

- [ ] How many failed logons came from appt01, for which account?
- [ ] When did the logon succeed, and with which Logon Type?
- [ ] Which share was opened, and which files were read?
- [ ] What kind of data is in that share? Why does that raise the stakes?

> Hint: The one 4625 on 5 Nov at 03:31 is the receptionist mistyping at the keyboard (Logon Type 2). It isn't part of this.

?> How many failed logons came from 10.30.1.20? :: sha256:19581e27de7ced00ff1ce50b2047e7a567c76b1cbaebabe5ef03f7c3017bb5b7
?> Which share did the attacker open on rcp-pc03? :: sha256:5982f892947ea523f3a9473a5af9ded238c1204127e1e595e845e7555ba6c99c
?> How many files were read from it? :: sha256:e7f6c011776e8db7cd330b54174fd76f7d0216b612387a5ffcfb81e6f0919683

## 8. A sensor rule for next time

Turn what you found into rules the IDS can run on every packet, so the next download and the next beacon raise an alert by themselves. Run them on the capture and check two things: they catch the bad traffic, and they don't fire on the portal, the backup or the database.

```tool ids
{"rules": "", "file": "capture.pcap", "n": 5, "blank": ["rules"], "a": {"rules": "alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:\"Script or binary fetched by wget or curl\"; http.user_agent; pcre:\"/^(Wget|curl)\\//\"; sid:1100001; rev:1;)\nalert tls $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 443 (msg:\"Beacon to cdn.patch-relay.example\"; content:\"SNI=cdn.patch-relay.example\"; sid:1100002; rev:1;)\n"}}
```

- [ ] Rule 1 catches both downloads
- [ ] Rule 2 catches the three beacons
- [ ] No alert on internal traffic
- [ ] One line on what each rule would miss

> Hint: A real server rarely needs Wget or curl to reach the internet, so those User-Agents are worth an alert there. A beacon rule on one server name is easy to evade with a new name; the timing is the more lasting sign.

?> How many alerts do the two rules give on the capture? :: sha256:ef2d127de37b942baad06145e54b0c619a1f22327b2ebbcfbec78f5564afe39d

## 9. Write the triage note and the network finding

Two short documents carry this to the next person: a **host triage note** for appt01 and a **network finding**. Each says what you checked, with the exact commands and filters, so anyone can repeat it. Keep facts apart from guesses.

```tool report
{"tpl": "triage", "title": "Triage note: appt01 compromised through SSH password guessing", "text": "", "n": 6, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Triage note: appt01 compromised through SSH password guessing

## What fired

IDS alert at 01:20:11 UTC on 6 Nov: script download by Wget from appt01 (10.30.1.20) to 203.0.113.77 (cdn.patch-relay.example).

## What I checked

- auth.log: `grep 'Failed password' auth.log | grep -o 'from [0-9.]*' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`, then `grep Accepted` and the sudo COMMAND lines.
- crontab.txt, ps.txt and recovered/m.sh.
- Capture: filters `http.request`, `ip.addr==203.0.113.77`, `tls and ip.dst==203.0.113.77`.
- Zeek conn.log pairs, and rcp-pc03's Security log (4625, 4624, 5140, 5145).

## What I found

- 46 failed SSH passwords from 198.51.100.23 between 01:02 and 01:19 UTC, then "Accepted password for vendor" at 01:19:44.
- As root (sudo), vendor fetched /m.sh with Wget at 01:20:10 and ran it. The script fetched /a.bin with curl into /usr/local/bin/.sysmon-agent and added a root cron job every 10 minutes.
- The program is running (PID 2644) and calls cdn.patch-relay.example over TLS every 10 minutes (01:21, 01:31, 01:41).
- At 01:33 appt01 tried frontdesk's password on rcp-pc03 nine times, got in at 01:34:02 and read six files from the Scans share.

## What I don't know yet

- What .sysmon-agent does; we have not analysed the binary.
- How the vendor account's password was guessable, and whether the vendor uses it elsewhere.
- How frontdesk's password was known: reused, guessed or stolen.
- Whether anything left the network apart from what the capture shows (it covers 01:15 to 01:45 only).

## Disposition and why

True positive, high: a server holding appointment data is controlled by an outsider, and patient scans were read on another machine.

## Next step and owner

- Clinic IT (now): take appt01 off the internet, disable vendor and frontdesk, keep a disk image before cleaning.
- Clinic manager (today): treat the Scans access as a possible personal data breach and start the notification checks.
- Vendor: support only through a VPN with keys, never a password on an open port.
"}}
```

```tool report
{"tpl": "triage", "title": "Triage note: network finding for 6 Nov, 01:00 to 02:00 UTC", "text": "", "n": 6, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Triage note: network finding for 6 Nov, 01:00 to 02:00 UTC

## What fired

Zeek and the IDS, reviewed together after the appt01 alert.
```
